title: Everyday Redesign Challenge
tagline: Measure · Find the cause · Fix the system
goal: Your kid picks something at home that bugs everyone, like lost shoes, a cluttered counter or the dinner rush. They measure it, interview the family, find the real cause, design a fix that makes the right thing the easy thing, then test it for a week and compare the numbers.
need: Paper and a pencil, and a timer
A problem the whole family agrees is annoying
Whatever the fix needs: a basket, hooks, labels, tape (use what you have first)

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Be an honest test subject. If your system is the one that isn't working, let them say so and let them change it for a week. Resist fixing their fix: the test will show what works, and that's more convincing than anything you could tell them.

plan.what: Pick the problem and start counting (Step 1).
Interview, find the cause and design the fix (Steps 2 to 4).
Test it, count again and compare (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: They want to redesign the whole house
troubleshoot.a: One problem, one fix. A small win in a week beats a big plan that never gets tested.
Ask why, and treat the answer as data. Usually the fix added a step. Make it easier, not stricter.

lesson.text: Most everyday problems aren't about people trying too little. They're about a system that makes the wrong thing easy.
lesson.before: Everyone needs to stop losing their shoes.

model.line: Shoes went missing 6 times this week, about 10 minutes each search.
Shoes come off at the kitchen door. The rack is by the front door.
A basket at the kitchen door, where shoes actually come off.
The next week: 1 missing shoe. From 6 to 1.

lesson.modelNote: Telling people to try harder changed nothing. Moving the basket to where shoes come off did, and the count proved it.

steps.title: Spot the problem and measure it
steps.why: A number turns 'this always happens' into something you can fix and check.
steps.kid: Your kid picks something at home that bugs everyone: lost keys or shoes, a cluttered counter, the dinner rush, chore arguments. Before changing anything, they measure it for 3 days, using the Measure it card in the Redesign Toolkit at the end of the guide: a tally mark each time it happens, or a timer on how long it takes.
steps.you: Be honest about what frustrates you too. Then leave things exactly as they are for three days, so the count is fair.
ask: What's the one thing people complain about most?
How often do you think it happens? Guess before you count.
steps.tip: Put the tally sheet right where the problem happens, with a pencil taped to it. If it's in a drawer, nobody counts.

levels.explore: Pick one thing that bugs you and make a tally mark every time it happens for a day.
levels.develop: Pick one problem and count or time it for 3 days.
levels.extend: Measure two ways, how often and how long, and turn it into minutes lost per week.

steps.title: Interview the people it affects
steps.why: Everyone sees the same problem a little differently.
steps.kid: Your kid asks each person it affects the same few questions: what bothers you most, when does it happen, have you tried to fix it, and what would 'fixed' look like? They write the answers down and look for what people agree on.
steps.you: Answer for real, even if the honest answer is 'I leave my things there too.' A kid who hears that gets better data than a kid who hears 'it's fine.'
ask: Does everyone even agree on what the problem is?
steps.tip: Interview the youngest too. Little kids often notice exactly where things go wrong.

levels.explore: Ask one person two questions, and tell me what they said.
levels.develop: Interview everyone it affects and find what most people agree on.
levels.extend: Find where people disagree about the problem itself, and decide whose problem you're solving first, and why.

steps.title: Find the real cause
steps.why: Fix the surface and it comes back. Fix the cause and it stays fixed.
steps.kid: Your kid watches the problem happen: where exactly, when, and what the person was doing. Then they ask 'why?' and keep asking, using the Five whys card, until they reach something they can change: a place, a step or a habit.
steps.you: Keep asking 'but why?' with them, and steer away from blame. 'Because he's messy' isn't a cause. 'Because the hook is too high to reach' is.
ask: Is it the space, the steps or the habit?
If we fixed only the surface, would it come back?
steps.tip: The real cause is usually a place. Things pile up where they're used, not where they're supposed to go.

levels.explore: Watch it happen once and say where and when it happened.
levels.develop: Do the five whys and write down the cause you can change.
levels.extend: Find two possible causes and test which matters more: change one for a day and see if the count drops.

steps.title: Design the fix
steps.why: The best fix makes the right thing easier than the wrong thing.
steps.kid: Your kid designs a fix using the Redesign rules card: put it where the problem happens, make it easier than the old way, use fewer steps, and make it easy to see. They sketch it, explain it to the family, then set it up with what's at home.
steps.you: Ask 'how would that actually work on a busy morning?' Help with anything that needs drilling or lifting, and let them run the rest.
ask: Would everyone actually use this, even in a hurry?
What's the one step you removed?
steps.tip: Use what you have first. A box, a hook or a strip of tape tells you if the idea works before anything gets bought.

levels.explore: Draw your fix and show it to the family.
levels.develop: Design the fix with the Redesign rules and set it up.
levels.extend: Design two fixes, a free one and one that costs something, and predict which will cut the count more.

steps.title: Test it for a week
steps.why: The numbers decide, not the opinions.
steps.kid: Your kid runs the fix for a week and counts again, the same way as before. Then they compare before and after, ask everyone how it felt, and make one change for Version 2. If it didn't work, the count shows where to look next.
steps.you: Follow the new system yourself, even if you'd have designed it differently. If you slip, let it show in the count.
ask: What were the numbers before and after?
What will you change for Version 2?
steps.tip: Count on the same days of the week as before. Weekends and weekdays are rarely the same.

levels.explore: Try the fix for 2 days, then tell me if it got better.
levels.develop: Run it for a week, count again and compare before and after.
levels.extend: Work out the percentage change, find the day it slipped, and explain why.

conclusion.headline: The fix stuck, and they have the numbers.
conclusion.text: Watch what they say the next time something at home annoys them. If 'where does it actually happen?' comes before 'whose fault is it?', the redesign habit has stuck.
conclusion.celebrate: Read the two numbers out loud together: 'Six times the week before, once this week. Your fix did that.'
extensions: Redesign a second problem someone else picks
Go back to the old way for two days to prove the fix made the difference
Redesign a space for a grandparent or a neighbour
Write a one-page how-to so the fix survives

signs: They point out when something is stored far from where it's used
They fix the system instead of blaming the person
makeItReal: Give them one household annoyance a month to redesign, from the bathroom towels to the recycling, and put the before and after numbers on the fridge.
